title: Newly Diagnosed Multiple Sclerosis Presenting as Brown-Séquard Syndrome: A Case Report
journal: Clinical Practice and Cases in Emergency Medicine
case_prompt:
A 25-year-old right-handed woman with no prior medical history presented with one week of right lower extremity numbness from toes to hip and three days of progressive left lower extremity weakness, resulting in use of crutches. She reported a minor fall onto an air mattress three days before the onset of weakness but denied significant trauma or other injuries. She had no fevers, chills, upper extremity symptoms, facial or visual changes, speech or swallowing difficulties.
On examination, she was alert and afebrile with normal cranial nerve function. Upper extremity strength and sensation were intact. In the lower extremities, left hip flexion was 3/5, knee extension 4/5, foot dorsiflexion 3/5, and plantarflexion 5/5; right lower extremity strength was 5/5 throughout. Sensory testing showed decreased pinprick and temperature on the right up to the T11–T12 dermatomes, and reduced proprioception and vibration in the left from mid-shin downward. Left patellar clonus was present with 6–7 beats; ankle jerks were symmetric, and Babinski and Hoffman signs were equivocal.
MRI of the spine demonstrated multifocal T2‐hyperintense lesions with contrast enhancement, suspicious for an inflammatory or demyelinating process, without space-occupying lesions. Brain MRI showed periventricular, juxtacortical, and infratentorial gadolinium-enhancing lesions. An axial T2‐weighted image at L1 revealed a high-signal lesion hemisecting the spinal cord.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Trauma was considered given the fall, but timing and severity made it unlikely — “the patient’s fall was likely coincidental in timing and largely unrelated to the development of her symptoms.”  
2. Cervical disc herniation was excluded by imaging — “Imaging ruled out etiologies such as cervical disc herniation…”  
3. Epidural hematoma was ruled out on MRI — “Imaging ruled out etiologies such as … epidural hematoma…”  
4. Syringomyelia was excluded by the absence of a cord cystic cavity — “Imaging ruled out etiologies such as … syringomyelia as a cause.”  
5. Tumors were unlikely given no mass lesions on imaging — “Imaging showed multifocal areas of T2 hyperintensity… without space-occupying lesions.”  
6. Neuromyelitis optica was considered among demyelinating causes but excluded by negative serologies — “Lesser known causes such as NMO … were ruled out through negative blood and cerebrospinal fluid … studies.”  
7. Infection was evaluated and excluded by CSF and serologic studies — “Lesser known causes such as … infection were ruled out through negative blood and cerebrospinal fluid … studies.”  
8. Multiple sclerosis was diagnosed based on characteristic MRI lesions and steroid response — “Given the patient’s classic findings of multiple sclerosis (MS) on both her head and spinal MRIs, steroids were started. This treatment resulted in significant resolution of her symptoms, confirming our suspicion of MS.”
